title: Quantifying the Accuracy and Precision of the Transition Dipole Moment Alignment from Realistic Angular Emission Data.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Introduction From solar cells to light emitting diodes
to sensors, the efficiency
of every optoelectronic device is inherently influenced by the angular
emission pattern of light. In photovoltaics, the maximum voltage and
efficiency of a solar cell is dictated by the etendue, or angular
spread of light emission from radiative recombination of the semiconductor.
Up to 10% in efficiency can be gained when the angular spread of light
from the sun is matched by the angular spread of light emitted by
the radiative recombination of the solar cell. 
 , 
  In
lighting and displays, the angular light emission determines how much
light is emitted from the device and defines the external quantum
efficiency (EQE). For example, organic light emitting diodes (OLEDs)
lose up to 80% of generated photons when light is emitted isotropically
as some light is emitted into angles that are trapped within the device
layers instead of emitted outward for viewing. 
 − 
 
 
  Thus, to maximize the efficiency
of these devices, we must maximize light emission into desired angles
and modes. Light emission is an inherently directional process.  Photons are generated during radiative recombination,
where electrons relax from higher energy to lower energy states. The
electron’s cycling between different energy levels generates
an inherent dipole moment (the transition dipole moment, or TDM) and
an anisotropic electric field, resulting in anisotropic light emission.
This directionality is not observed in many bulk materials: most bulk
materials have many energetic states with equal strengths in all directions,
thus resulting in a completely isotropic emission pattern. However,
this directionality can be observed in materials that only support
individual states, such as dye molecules,  in materials with confined, quantized states, such as quantum dots 
 , 
  and 2D films,  and in nanomaterials
that are highly responsive to their environment. 
 − 
 
 
  Using these directionally emitting
materials in optoelectronic devices can overcome the entropic losses
discussed earlier and yield significant device efficiency gains. 
 , − 
 
 
 The angular light emission pattern, 
 , , − 
 , − 
 
 
  light absorption or emission polarization, 
 , 
  and photoluminescence lifetime 
 − 
 
 
  all provide insight into the
alignment and relative strength of the transition dipole moments of
a sample. Resolving the effective dipole alignment through the angular
emission pattern is a popular method for characterizing simple thin
film samples, for example by (1) using a light detector that directly
collects the light emission at different angles;  or (2) inserting a simple lens into the pathway of a microscope
that changes the focal plane to the Fourier plane of the microscope,
providing a 2D projection of the 3D angular emission pattern, known
as back focal plane imaging or momentum-resolved spectroscopy.  The fitted transition dipole moment from this
measurement represents the statistical average of all the transition
dipole moments in the emitting layer. For a simple optical environment,
such as a thin emissive layer
(film thickness ≪ emission wavelength) on a planar substrate,
the angular emission pattern is well-described by a 1D analytical
solution that modifies the dipole emission pattern by interaction
with the two interfaces (film-vacuum, film–substrate) and propagation
through the film. Example projections of angular emission patterns
for various dipole alignments are shown in  Figure  
 C. The dipole alignment is typically determined
by finding the best fit between the experimental angular emission
pattern and the calculated patterns of various dipole alignments.
However, the best fit is not always obvious:  Figure  
 C shows that the angular emission patterns
look very similar when the dipole is aligned more parallel to the
substrate. This can be a significant challenge for predicting the
device performance; even very subtle changes in the anisotropy of
the electric dipoles can have an immense impact on the device efficiency.
For example, the external quantum efficiency of an OLED is 24.7% higher
for an emitter where the effective dipole alignment angle is 8°
closer to the substrate than a purely isotropic emitter (average effective
angle 35.3°).  Despite this range
in performance, the uncertainty of this fitting procedure is typically
not reported. Further, the inherent or expected error of this fitting
procedure has not yet been widely quantified. Therefore, there is
a great need to not only determine the dipole alignments of candidate
materials but also to know the precision of these dipole alignments
to give an accurate prediction and range of device performance. 1 (a) 3-layer
schematic showing air, the emissive film, and substrate.
The effective transition dipole moment (TDM eff ) angle is
the angle between the substrate and the in-plane and out-of-plane
dipole contributions. The thickness of the film (D) is assumed to
be smaller than the emission wavelength of light (λ). The dashed
pink lines represent the in-plane and out-of-plane dipoles that contribute
to the effective transition dipole moment. (b) 3D angular emission
pattern (black wireframe) from a dipole (purple arrow) in free space.
Emission is defined in spherical coordinates (θ. ϕ). (c)
Projected x-polarized angular emission patterns of a dipole from the
3-layer model for different TDM eff  angle orientations with
respect to the normalized momentum vectors  k

 ,  k 
 
 y 
 . The toroid-shape of the dipole is modified by the air–film
and film–substrate interfaces. The angular emission pattern
appears very similar for low effective transition dipole moment angles
(TDM eff  ≤ 30°). In this work, we apply a statistical method to
evaluate the accuracy
and precision of measuring the dipole alignment from the fitting to
angular emission patterns. First, we quantify the fundamental precision
for this type of measurement using Monte Carlo simulations to add
random noise to theoretical angular emission patterns. We show that
the confidence intervals are not constant across samples, and there
is an increased associated uncertainty for films with most dipoles
aligned close to the substrate and for films with higher refractive
index ( n 
 2  ≥ 3). Next, we explore
the inherent difficulties of finding an accurate fit, or where the
best fit data set matches the correct underlying parameters. We show
that accurately determining the correct transition dipole moment alignment
is possible, albeit challenging, when additional parameters of the
emitting layer are unknown (thickness, refractive index) using rigorous
optimization methods such as simulated annealing. Finally, we show
that pixel bleeding and blurring that typically appear in experimental
angular emission patterns obfuscate the true transition dipole moment
alignment from the experimentally best-fit values, preventing accurate
characterization. We showed that incorporating such nonidealities
in angular emission patterns can lead to enormous differences (>10°)
between the best fit effective TDM angle and the true effective TDM
angle, and this is exacerbated again for thin films with high refractive
indices ( n 
 2  ≥ 2). We offer an improved
and physics-motivated protocol for processing experimental data by
selecting a specific subset of the angular emission data, which allows
us to achieve much more accurate fits than the traditional methods
of fitting just the p-polarized linecuts or the entire angular space.
Thus, this work provides a procedure both for quantifying the precision
of characterizing the transition dipole moment alignment and for ensuring
more accurate alignment measurements when experimental nonidealities
are present.

sections.heading: The Generation of Theoretical Angular Emission Patterns
sections.text:
The Generation of Theoretical Angular Emission Patterns In this work, we used artificially generated data sets of the photoluminescence
intensity as a function of photon momentum and several underlying
parameters. These data sets can then be fed into subsequent statistical
models to quantify accuracy and precision. The angular light emission
pattern from dipoles within a thin film is well described by a simple
three-layer analytical model. 
 , , , , 
 
 Figure  
 A shows the
setup with the three layers: (1) the background media (usually assumed
to be air), (2) the emissive thin film where the thickness of the
film is smaller than the wavelength of emitted light, and (3) the
substrate (usually glass). This analysis is generalized to assume
that horizontal dipole contributions are degenerate, meaning there
are horizontal dipoles along the x- and  y -directions.
Most derivations assume a polarizer is used during the measurement
because this removes one of the horizontal dipole contributions (here
applied in the  x -direction) and allows the average
dipole orientation, or the difference between horizontal and vertical
dipole contributions, be better resolved. Here, we use the following
general equation for the polarized light emission intensity projected
onto a 2-D collection plane ( N

TDM eff  = 90° corresponds to completely out-of-plane

dipole emission has a toroidal
shape which has no light emission along the dipole axis and maximum
light emission perpendicular to it (see  Figure  
 B). This uniform emission pattern is then
modified by the reflection and transmission through the surrounding
interfaces. Example x-polarized angular emission patterns for different
TDM eff  angles are provided in  Figure  
 C. We include the x-polarizer to better resolve
the in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, which removes
the azimuthal symmetry in the 90° case and one of the degenerate
horizontal dipoles. Lower TDM eff  angles (aligned parallel
to substrate) have strong minima along the  k 
 
 x 
  direction while higher TDM eff  angles (aligned perpendicular to the substrate) have low emission
in the center ( k

  =  k

  = 0). In this work,
we generated angular emission patterns from this
theoretical framework to determine the accuracy and precision of a
fitted effective transition dipole moment angle. We investigated four
example refractive indices, n 2  = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0,
to represent classes of materials (air, organic materials, low refractive

film thicknesses (10, 20, 50, and 100 nm) and three emission wavelengths
(400, 515, and 1000 nm) to represent visible to NIR emitting structures.
After generating these angular emission patterns, we applied further
processing to mimic the nonidealities of real experimental data. These
generated data sets were then compared against the basic theory to
quantify the inherent accuracy and precision of this technique.
